analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office to manufacture affordable insulin, inhalers, EpiPens, naloxone, and antibiotics.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its initial referral: introduced in the Senate in December 2023 and sent to the health committee, it received no further action before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. That office would manufacture or contract for the production of prescription drugs that are expensive, in short supply, or sold by only a few companies — starting with insulin in every dosage form, asthma and COPD inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors (like EpiPens), naloxone, and antibiotics. The office would sell these drugs at a publicly set 'fair price,' publish all its prices, and could sell its FDA approvals to other manufacturers on the condition they keep prices low. It would also bar former drug industry lobbyists and executives of companies under federal enforcement actions from working there for six years.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay high prices for insulin, inhalers, EpiPens, and naloxone; people affected by drug shortages; taxpayers and Federal and State health programs like Medicare, Medicaid, and the VA, which would buy from the office; and smaller pharmacies and clinics that could gain a reliable low-cost supplier.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients who overpay for essential drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires the office to begin publicly manufacturing at least one insulin product of each dosage form and type, at least one inhaler, an epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone, and at least three antibiotics within one year of enactment

Requires the office to sell drugs it makes at a 'fair price' that accounts for patient access, the cost to Federal and State health programs, and manufacturing cost, and to publish all prices it pays and charges

Directs the office to prioritize drugs that would most lower patient costs, fix shortages, improve public health, and address health disparities, and to reach at least 15 manufactured drugs within one year and 25 within three
Bars former registered drug industry lobbyists and former senior executives of companies under federal enforcement settlements from being hired by the office for six years
Requires the VA, Defense Department, Public Health Service, and Coast Guard to buy minimum amounts of drugs made by the office

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would face a new government-owned competitor in markets where few companies sell. Taxpayers would fund the office's startup and manufacturing costs, which the bill authorizes as 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and taxpayers funding the office

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in appropriations with no dollar limit, so the startup and operating cost of a federal drug manufacturing operation is open-ended

The one-year deadlines are demanding: the office must be running, file FDA applications for multiple products, and begin manufacturing at least 15 drugs within a year, which is far faster than typical FDA approval timelines allow

A common objection to public manufacturing is that the federal government has limited experience running pharmaceutical plants and that quality, recall, and financial risks would fall on taxpayers; the bill's own structure acknowledges this by allowing the office to contract manufacturing out, mostly to nonprofit and public partners

The office's authority to acquire manufacturing rights under federal licensing authorities such as march-in rights could reduce the returns that drug companies expect on new medicines, which critics argue would discourage investment in research

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is concrete and targeted: cheaper insulin, inhalers, EpiPens, naloxone, and antibiotics, plus a government backstop against shortages. The main risks are cost and execution — an open-ended appropriation, aggressive deadlines, and a federal agency entering a manufacturing business it has never run. The bill hedges by preferring contracts with nonprofit and public manufacturers and by requiring annual public reporting, but whether it would deliver savings quickly enough to justify the cost is a fair question.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill in the Senate on December 5, 2023, with Senator Jeff Merkley
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
No further action — no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the record before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025
The bill had one cosponsor listed in addition to the sponsor

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Existing drug manufacturers, who continue to face no public competitor in the insulin, inhaler, epinephrine, naloxone, and antibiotic markets, while patients and health programs keep paying current prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers; patients keep paying

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Affordable Drug Manufacturing Act of 2023 in the Senate

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's sponsors and cosponsor were all Democrats, so it never attracted the bipartisan support that moves a bill to the floor.

industries.note: A government office would manufacture low-cost versions of their drugs — starting with insulin, inhalers, and epinephrine auto-injectors — and sell them at a publicly set fair price, directly undercutting their prices in markets where few companies sell. Their gain in the outcome is the status quo: no public competitor was created.

The bill specifically requires public manufacturing of at least one insulin product of every dosage form and type within a year, a direct challenge to a market dominated by a few companies with repeatedly rising prices.

A government manufacturer would be a new competitor, but the office must also sell its approved applications to any buyer who commits to making the drug and keeping prices low — which could hand generic makers an FDA approval at low cost. Companies that fail to market the drug or raise prices lose the application back to the office.

industries.industry: Drug wholesalers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The office must sell through wholesalers at a fair price and includes wholesalers and PBMs on its advisory council, so their distribution role continues; but published prices and a low-cost public supplier would squeeze the margin between what manufacturers charge and what payers receive.
